opening.headline: Learn the development flow of evaluation-based development where quality improvements after changing prompts or models are verified with visible evidence.
body: After modifying the prompt by just one line, one person says they've improved significantly, while another says the previous version was better. Since generative AI can produce different outputs even with the same input, judging changes based solely on personal experience after trying it a few times is insufficient to determine the impact of the modification.

In this course, we examine the development process centered on evaluation. The sequence involves setting objectives, collecting evaluation data, defining metrics, implementing and comparing results, and then re-evaluating whenever changes are made. We also distinguish the points at which evaluation informs design decisions, and follow through the process of identifying regression—where prompt modifications worsen certain questions.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the flow of evaluation-based development.
It is possible to distinguish the point at which evaluation contributes to design decisions.

screens.title: I modified the prompt, but I don't know if it improved.
screens.lead: First, read the scene many teams encounter. While reading, consider why the two judgments differ and what evidence is missing.

visual.alt: A scene where two people express opposing impressions regarding the same prompt change.
labels: It has improved greatly. The refund inquiry responses have become more courteous.
Earlier was better. The order cancellation inquiry comes out strangely.
No evaluation results serving as basis

paragraphs: A team improved their refund inquiry classification prompt to be more friendly. One team member said that after directly adding a few refund inquiries, the results improved significantly. Another team member reported that they received strange results when handling order cancellation inquiries and said the previous version performed better. Both individuals are not wrong—each observed a few cases where the current version produced accurate results.

Traditional software produces the same output for the same input, so it can be verified with predefined tests. In contrast, generative AI may produce different outputs even for the same input. The OpenAI evaluation guide explains that because of this variability, traditional software testing methods are insufficient, and evaluation—referred to as "evals"—is needed to compensate.

What this team needs right now is not just more effort in trying out questions. It's evidence that compares pre- and post-change questions within the same set of queries, showing which questions have improved and which have deteriorated.

callout.label: Questions for this class
callout.text: How can the impact of changes on quality be made visible through tangible evidence?

screens.outro: First, let's consider whether there is an evaluation comparing changes against the current service.

screens.title: Think about whether there is an evaluation comparing before and after changes.
screens.lead: First, think carefully about the question on your own and then choose. No content is entered or submitted; instead, what appears is the instructor's summary of thoughts.

items.prompt: Do you have a list of questions to verify changes?
items.answer: If there is no list, we would have to repeatedly verify with different questions, making it impossible to compare results. Using the same set of questions consistently serves as the starting point for comparison. Even a small list of ten or so items at the beginning is acceptable.

items.prompt: Does this list resemble actual user requests?
items.answer: The evaluation data will differ from real traffic if it contains only questions that developers have thought of. The OpenAI guide identifies the failure to accurately reproduce the distribution of operational environments in evaluation data as an anti-pattern known as biased design. Real questions extracted from logs serve as excellent material.

items.prompt: Is the criterion for good answers and bad answers written out in sentences?
items.answer: If the standard exists only in one's mind, people may reach different judgments. It can be written out as a sentence so that others can evaluate it against the same standard, or it can be transferred in a way that is automatically verified later.

screens.outro: Now, let's examine the overall flow of evaluation-based development step by step.

screens.title: The flow of assessment, amendment, and re-assessment
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to sequentially review the five stages of evaluation-based development. Pay attention to what is defined and what is left out at each stage.

visual.alt: A five-step cyclical process: goal, data, metrics, action, and continuous evaluation.

steps.title: Define the first-stage objective.
steps.body: First, define the success criteria that evaluations must pass. For example, in query classification, the goal is for the model to return a single label that matches the intent of the question. If the goal is vague, the data and metrics in subsequent stages will also become vague. Early and frequent evaluation, along with narrow-scope tests at each stage, is the essence of evaluation-driven development.

steps.title: Collect the dataset for stage 2 evaluation
steps.body: This collects data that can confirm goals. Examples of expected answers created by experts, past questions retrieved from operational logs, and data with user feedback are candidates. The data should include not only typical cases but also edge cases and adversarial cases. By preserving logs, we can later identify good evaluation examples.

steps.title: Define the third-stage indicator.
steps.body: Specifies how to verify whether the goal has been achieved. The example of document question-answering from the OpenAI Guide lists goal-specific criteria such as context reproduction rate of 0.85 or higher, precision exceeding 0.7, and positive evaluation responses at 70% or above. Only one number should not be considered; judgments must be made in conjunction with human evaluation. It is explained that a more stable approach is to evaluate whether one response is better than the other or to make judgments based on predefined criteria, rather than simply assessing whether the model produces fluent free-form responses.

steps.title: Step 4: Execute and compare.
steps.body: Run the evaluation dataset to record results and compare changes item by item. The comparison must be made under the same evaluation set and identical execution conditions to be meaningful. Simply looking at averages may obscure deterioration in certain items, so we must examine results at the item level. At this stage, we first need to establish a baseline for the pre-change state using the same evaluation set, in order to subsequently compare the changes.

steps.title: Evaluates continuously after every fifth change.
steps.body: Continuous evaluation is the process of running evaluations whenever changes occur, monitoring the service, and gradually enriching the evaluation set with newly discovered variation cases. Performing evaluations only once before release or relying on the perception that the system is working well are anti-patterns documented in this text.

steps.title: Release Baseline and Regression Verification
steps.body: The release criterion is a predefined statement that specifies when a release is deemed acceptable—namely, when the condition is met. Regression testing involves re-evaluating the same set of test cases to verify that items which previously passed continue to pass after a change. By pre-defining both the release criterion and the regression test suite, a decision about whether to release a change can be made based on objective criteria rather than subjective judgment.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the flow, let's structurally distinguish the points at which evaluation can assist in design decisions.

screens.title: The point at which evaluation contributes to design decisions
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the points where uncertainty arises by service structure with the evaluation criteria.

tabs.label: Single call
tabs.body:
This is a structure where user input goes into the model and produces a single output. For example, when the system prompt classifies a customer's question into one of the categories: order_status, return_policy, technical_issue, cancel_order, or other.

Uncertainty arises in two places. First, when evaluating compliance with instructions provided by developers and users, we check whether the model prioritizes the system prompt over the user request and whether it focuses on the classification task. Second, when evaluating functional accuracy of the model's output, we assess whether the model's inferred intent matches the intended intent.

tabs.label: workflow
tabs.body:
This is a structure that chains together multiple model invocations. According to the documentation, the workflow introduces no new uncertainties, but since it involves interactions between multiple models, each step can be evaluated separately.

In the case of querying order status, the three steps—extracting the order number, retrieving order information, and generating the final response—are individually reviewed. By evaluating each step, we can narrow down where the quality deteriorates, providing the basis for determining where improvements are needed.

tabs.label: agent
tabs.body:
In a structure where the model selects tools and sequentially chains multiple steps on its own, evaluation points increase. The more complex the structure, the more locations where uncertainty arises, and thus the greater the number of places that require evaluation.

The principle of documentation is to evaluate at the points where uncertainty occurs. It is practical to first establish evaluation at the single-call level before the structure becomes complex, and then gradually add evaluations at each point as the structure grows.

tabs.label: Selecting Improvement Methods
tabs.body:
OpenAI's accuracy optimization documentation describes prompt improvement, retrieval augmentation (RAG), and fine-tuning as means for addressing different problems. If a model lacks contextual knowledge, it should be augmented with context; if the model's format or tone is inconsistent, its behavior must be refined.

Therefore, first establish baselines using prompts and evaluation, examine the root causes of errors, and then select appropriate methods. Additionally, assess the cost of failures against the benefits of successes to determine when a solution is sufficiently good.

screens.outro: Since we have distinguished the location of the evaluation, let's proceed with an example where changes have exacerbated certain questions.

screens.title: Case Explanation: When Prompt Changes Worsened Certain Questions
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the prompt modification example step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. The question set and results for the example are assumed for illustrative purposes.

steps.title: See case
steps.body: After improving the customer inquiry classification prompt to be more friendly, the response to refund inquiries looked much better. The team wants to deploy quickly, but has decided first to verify it on the evaluation set. Classification involves assigning exactly one label per question. I will follow this example to verify at what point the evaluation provides relevant information.

steps.title: Step 1: Create a reference line
steps.body: Before making any changes, run the entire evaluation set once to record results per item. This record serves as the baseline for comparison. Without a baseline, it is impossible to determine whether the results after changes are good or bad. For each item, keep track of which label was assigned and whether it was correct or incorrect.

steps.title: Step 2: Change the Prompt
steps.body: We are modifying the prompt. This change includes adding instructions to make the explanation more kind. To narrow down the cause, we must only compare the results for this single change and refrain from altering any other elements. If we change multiple aspects at once, we will not be able to determine what caused the difference in results.

steps.title: Re-evaluate using a similar evaluation set from stage 3.
steps.body: Run the same evaluation set again to compare item by item. Changing the evaluation set or running only a subset can blur the comparison, so it's important to execute under the same conditions as before. Output may vary, so run multiple times if necessary to observe trends.

steps.title: Step 4: Discover Regression
steps.body: The overall average is similar. However, on a per-item basis, some technical issues and a portion of order cancellation inquiries are being classified under different labels. The average has remained stable due to an increase in refund-related queries, which has masked some deterioration in the average. This would have been missed if a per-item comparison had not been conducted.

steps.title: Step 5: Perform Root Cause Analysis
steps.body: Let's examine a categorized example directly. We confirm that the reason the new instruction weakens the requirement to first provide a friendly explanation and then merely return the label is due to this. Once the cause is identified, the direction for correction becomes clear. For instance, we could try placing the instruction to merely return the label earlier or adding additional examples.

steps.title: Step 6: Make a Decision
steps.body: Since it does not meet the release criteria, changes are either revised or deferred. Because the criteria were predefined, even though there has been an increase in refund inquiries, the release decision can be made without hesitation. The revised prompt returns to a cyclic comparison against the original stage-one benchmark.

steps.title: Step 7: Extend the Evaluation Dataset
steps.body: Add the discovered cases to the evaluation set. This way, when the same type of regression occurs again, it will be immediately apparent. The evaluation set is not something created once and then finished; instead, it grows and evolves alongside changes and accumulated cases. The two types of issues discovered in this case are now permanent parts of the evaluation set.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the benchmarks obtained from the case study.

screens.title: Evaluation is the safety net of design.
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lesson. Recall how to transform the initial question into visible evidence of impact, and read through it accordingly.

paragraphs: Generative AI can produce different outputs even with the same input, so relying solely on trial-and-error based on personal perception cannot reveal the effects of changes. Evaluation involves structured tests that enable systematic inspection of the system amidst this variability.

Evaluation-based development proceeds through the flow of goal definition, data collection, metric definition, execution comparison, and continuous evaluation. The evaluation set should resemble the distribution of real traffic and must include not only typical cases but also edge cases and adversarial cases. Metrics are read not just as numerical values but in conjunction with human judgment.

Evaluation is needed wherever variability is introduced. For a single call, compliance and functional accuracy are reported; in workflows, evaluation is performed step-by-step, and as the structure becomes more complex—like that of an agent—the number of evaluation points increases. By re-running the same evaluation suite each time changes are made and comparing results item by item, average performance can reveal regression issues that might otherwise be hidden.

Therefore, evaluation is not a gate at launch but a safety net kept alongside the entire development process. By setting release criteria in advance, you can decide whether to release based on standards rather than impressions.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Before making changes, establish a baseline, and after making changes, perform item-by-item comparisons using the same evaluation set. Looking at only the average may overlook some deterioration. Item-by-item comparison is the most direct way to detect regression, and remembering this alone greatly enhances the effectiveness of evaluation.

glossary.def: This is a development approach where you verify results with feedback after each change. You perform early, frequent, and narrowly scoped tests.
A collection of inputs and expected outcomes used for evaluation. It should resemble the distribution of actual traffic.
After the change, it's a verification to ensure that items that previously matched are still correct using the same evaluation set.
This is a predefined criterion that specifies the level at which changes can be exported.
This is a property where the output can differ even with the same input. This is why evaluation is necessary.

misconceptions.myth: Try it a few times; if it works well, that's sufficient.
misconceptions.fact: Since the output varies, it cannot be determined based on a few observations. A comparison before and after the change must be made using a predefined evaluation set.

misconceptions.myth: It's fine if they are equal.
misconceptions.fact: Some regressions worsening certain questions may be obscured by improvements in other questions. They must be examined item by item.

misconceptions.myth: Evaluation is done once, just before release.
misconceptions.fact: Assessments should be conducted early, frequently, and each time there are changes. Assessments should also be continued by adding newly discovered cases after release.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Evaluation is the safety net of the design.
The evaluation set resembles the actual distribution and includes boundary cases and adversarial cases.
Each time changes are made, the evaluation set is re-evaluated to compare item by item and verify regressions.
If you predefined the release criteria beforehand, the outcome can be determined by those criteria rather than by impression.
closing.reflectionLead: This question is intended to encourage you to think through it on your own. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What are the criteria that distinguish good from bad responses in my service, and what is needed to turn these into an evaluation dataset?

checks.q: Let's look at the flow of evaluation-based development in the correct order.
items: Run it and compare the results.
Evaluates continuously whenever there is a change
checks.explain: Start from the goal, create a evaluation set and metrics that resemble the actual distribution, execute the comparison, and then repeat the process in the same way each time modifications are made.
checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: After modifying the prompt, the overall average remains similar, but some questions are classified under different labels. What is the most important habit for detecting this?
options: Deploy after trying it a few times and finding it satisfactory.
Evaluates the same dataset before and after the change, comparing results item by item.
Only verify one average and if it matches, consider the issue resolved.
checks.explain: A regression where some items worsen, even if the average remains the same, might be obscured. To reveal it, you need to re-run the evaluation set each time and compare item-by-item.

wrong.0: It cannot be judged based on a few trials due to output volatility.
wrong.2: The average can help identify the worsening of some questions.
wrong.3: Evaluation should be done early, frequently, and each time after changes.
